answer:
The only way people can be “expelled from a natural boundary” is by a violent or forced removal that takes them across that boundary.  
In the case that the question is referring to, the “same people” who, during the reign of the Ajuran Sultanate, were driven out (in that period the Ajuran expelled the Portuguese – the “independence” episode that is usually mentioned in the historiography of the empire) turned up on the opposite side of the Mekong River, at Ban Pakpo in Vientiane Province, Laos.

That expulsion did not happen by a single battle or by a treaty; it was the result of a coordinated set–up by the Siamese (Thai) authorities in the late nineteenth‑early twentieth‑century.  In short:  

| What happened | How it happened | Where it ended up |
|---------------|----------------|------------------|
| **Forceful relocation** | Siamese troops moved along the paddy fields and river banks that constitute the natural border between Thailand and Laos – namely the Mekong – and escorted (or compelled) the expelled people across the river. | Ban Pakpo, a former Lao settlement on the Lao side of Route 13, just north of Vang Vieng. |

In other words, the people were literally expelled **by boat (or by marching on foot, following the river’s course) across the Mekong** – the river that forms the natural border – and were resettled in the village that now bears the name Ban Pakpo. The mechanism was a military‑sponsored relocation, not a voluntary migration or diplomatic exchange.
